title: New Grub Street: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to New Grub Street Unpacked — a close reading of George Gissing's extraordinary novel about writing, money, and the cost of both.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to go deep into one of the most clear-eyed, bracingly uncomfortable novels about literary life ever written.
New Grub Street was published in 1891, and it reads like it was written last Tuesday.
Joining me today are three people who know this novel with the kind of intimacy that makes conversation genuinely dangerous.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose obsession is craft — how the architecture of a sentence does moral and emotional work.
Eleanor, welcome.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions literature depicts — and what those institutions actually did to people.
He has a gift for righteous anger expressed at extremely low volume.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read New Grub Street as a teenager and has been re-reading it ever since — with, I suspect, increasing sympathy for almost everyone in it.
Caroline, welcome.
I want to start with Jasper Milvain — because he is, frankly, magnetic.
Caroline, before we get into the big arguments, will you just read us that line — the one I couldn't get out of my head after our conversation?
'To please the vulgar you must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity.'
Is Jasper being brilliantly honest there, or has he just confessed to something awful?
Both, I think — and that's precisely the trap Gissing sets for us from the very first pages.
Because when you read it in context — and let me read it properly — Jasper isn't sneering.
'To please the vulgar you must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity.'
He's almost admiring the difficulty of it.
There's a paradox buried in that phrase — 'genius of vulgarity' — that keeps me returning to it.
Genius isn't an insult here; Jasper is saying it takes real skill to serve the market well.
And that seductiveness — the feeling that he might just be right — is, I think, precisely what makes Jasper the most dangerous character in the novel.
I'd call it the most damning thing he says about himself — and I mean that structurally, not morally.

Jasper isn't wrong about the market — in 1891 the three-volume novel was collapsing, the circulating libraries were losing their grip, and the mass-market periodical press was absolutely ravenous for copy.
He's describing iron reality.
But notice what he also says — listen to the full shape of his argument.
'We are not geniuses, and if we sit down in a spirit of long-eared gravity we shall produce only commonplace stuff.'
He's already foreclosed the alternative — dismissed integrity before he's considered it.
That's not honesty — that's rationalisation dressed in the clothes of honesty.
But James — isn't that exactly what makes him seductive rather than damnable?
The rationalisation is so lucid, so well-constructed, that it does the work of argument.
Jasper isn't lying to himself in the dark — he's lying in the light, with style.
And I think Gissing wants us to feel the pull of that before he shows us the cost.
Can I say something about the sentences themselves, because I think you're both reading a moral argument and there's an architectural one running underneath it.
Look at the rhythm of Jasper's speech — short declarative blows followed by qualifications.
'It needs skill, mind you: and to deny it is a gross error of the literary pedants.'
That 'mind you' is doing extraordinary work — it's Jasper pre-empting the objection, acknowledging it exists, and dismissing it in the same breath.
Gissing has built a character whose syntax is itself a form of manipulation.
So when James says it's rationalisation and Caroline says it's seductive, they're both responding to the same formal effect — just naming it differently.
Eleanor, that's the intervention I wanted — because James is bringing the institutions and Caroline is reading the rhetoric, and you're saying those are the same thing.
James, I want to push on that — because you've said before that understanding the literary marketplace of the 1890s actually changes how we read Jasper's confidence.
Is Jasper confessing, or is he just describing reality more accurately than anyone else in the room?
He's describing reality accurately — I'll give Caroline that much.
The institutions of literary production in the 1880s and 90s were genuinely brutal in their commercial logic — and Jasper has read them precisely.
But accuracy about a brutal system is not the same as wisdom about it.
What Jasper never entertains — and the novel does entertain it, through Reardon — is whether you might refuse the system even at catastrophic cost.
And Reardon doesn't refuse it heroically — he just breaks under it.
Which is perhaps more honest than either refusal or capitulation.
And that's exactly where the formal question bites hardest.
Because in the passage where Reardon speaks about the weight dragging men down, the syntax does something completely different from Jasper's syntax.
'The world has no pity on a man who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money.'
That sentence isn't performing — it's collapsing.
The periodic structure — the long conditional 'who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money' — enacts the very weight Reardon is describing.
Jasper's sentences expand and assert; Reardon's sentences accumulate and press down.
Gissing is writing two incompatible experiences of the same world in two formally incompatible styles.
That passage hits me every time — every single re-read.
Because Reardon doesn't spare himself — he says 'I have no right to complain of my own ill-fortune; it's my own fault.'
'I have no right to complain of my own ill-fortune; it's my own fault (in a sense) that I can't continue as well as I began.'
That parenthetical — 'in a sense' — breaks my heart every time.
He's trying so hard to be fair to the world that destroyed him.
And then he can't hold it — 'Society is as blind and brutal as fate.'
'Society is as blind and brutal as fate.'
Five words and it's the whole novel.
James, you called the narrator's voice in chapter thirty-one prosecutorial — the passage that defends Reardon and Biffen directly against the world's judgement.
Is there a version where your reading, Eleanor's structural one, and Caroline's emotional one are all describing the same thing — or is there a real fight here about what Gissing actually believed?
There is a real fight, but it's one Gissing himself was having — and the narrator's voice in that chapter is where it becomes impossible to dodge.
The narrator steps out of the fiction and makes a direct indictment.
'From the familiar point of view these men were worthless; view them in possible relation to a humane order of Society, and they are admirable citizens.'
That phrase — 'a humane order of Society' — is doing enormous ideological work.
It posits a society that does not yet exist as the standard by which the existing one is found wanting.
That is a political argument in the clothes of a character defence — and I don't think Caroline or Eleanor would disagree with that.
I don't disagree — but I want to push back on 'prosecutorial,' because prosecutions have targets and verdicts, and this passage resists both.
Listen to how it ends.
'These two were richly endowed with the kindly and the imaginative virtues; if fate threw them amid incongruous circumstances, is their endowment of less value?'
It ends on a question — not a verdict.
A prosecution that ends with a question isn't prosecuting — it's asking you to hold two incompatible judgements simultaneously.
That's architecturally much more radical — and much harder to shake.
For me, that passage is the moral spine — but Eleanor is right that it doesn't resolve.
'You scorn their passivity; but it was their nature and their merit to be passive.'
That 'you' — direct address to the reader — is Gissing refusing to let us off.
We are implicated in the scorn.
And I think that's where all three readings converge — whether it's the institution, the syntax, or the emotional truth, the reader is always the one being judged.
And I think that's exactly where we should sit for a moment — with that implication, that weight.
Thank you all — Eleanor, James, Caroline — for a conversation that's already making me want to go back to the novel with fresh eyes.
When we come back, we're going to follow Reardon deeper into his spiral — the architecture of a writer's decline, sentence by sentence.

segments.title: The Architecture of Decline: Reardon's Spiral

utterances.text: We've been talking about the trap Grub Street sets — the market, the machinery, the slow grinding of literary ambition into commodity.
Now I want to go inside that trap and watch it close around one man in particular — Edwin Reardon.
And the thing that makes Reardon so unbearable to read — in the best sense — is that we watch the collapse happen at the level of the sentence.
Not just in the plot, not just in his marriage or his finances, but in the actual prose he's producing.
Gissing gives us a passage that is almost unbearably precise about what bad writing feels like from the inside.
Eleanor, I want you to read us that broken phrase — the one that starts 'She took a book with a look of—' — because I think people need to hear it spoken.
And I have to ask: is that dash actually good writing? Because on the surface it looks like Gissing just lost the thread.
Right, so let me read the full sequence, because the context is everything.
'His brain would not work; he could not recall the simplest synonyms; intolerable faults of composition drove him mad. He would write a sentence beginning thus: She took a book with a look of—'
That dash is not Gissing losing the thread — that dash is Gissing enacting exactly what he's describing.
The sentence literally cannot finish itself. The breakdown in Reardon's craft is performed inside Gissing's craft.
That's not an accident — that's an extraordinarily composed act of controlled illegibility.
I'll grant you the formal elegance of the move — and it is elegant.
But I wonder if 'composed illegibility' is doing rather too much work as a framing.
Because there's a prior question, which is: why is his brain failing him at all?
Reardon himself answers it quite precisely, and it isn't a mystery of artistic temperament — it's a material fact.
He says — and this is Reardon speaking directly —

'The probability is that this wouldn't matter, if only I could live on in peace of mind; I should recover my equilibrium, and perhaps once more understand myself. But the due course of things is troubled by my poverty.'
The broken syntax is downstream of the broken finances. Eleanor's formal reading is beautiful, but the cause is economic.
I don't dispute the economic causality for a moment — Gissing is absolutely insistent on it.
But to say the formal collapse is merely downstream of the money is to miss what Gissing is doing with his art.
The novel could have told us Reardon was failing without ever showing us his broken prose.
The choice to show us the galloping rhythm, the accidental rhyme, the sentence that can't complete itself — that's a separate and deliberate artistic decision.
And it matters because it makes us feel what it's like to be him — not just understand his situation from the outside.
What I keep coming back to is the effort.
He knows the writing is bad. He has what Gissing calls 'an appreciation of shapely prose' — and he's watching himself produce the opposite.
And yet he keeps going. The line that destroys me every time is at the very end of that passage.
'I can't help it; it must go; the time is passing.'
Those three short clauses. No ornament. Just endurance.
That, to me, is where the heart of it lives — not in the economics, not in the formal architecture, but in that bare human act of pushing forward when everything is failing.
James, you've argued that poverty is the real antagonist here — not Amy, not Reardon's temperament, not his standards.
But Caroline is pointing at something that looks like integrity — a conscience that won't let him write badly without feeling it.
So here's my question: is his integrity a virtue — or is it a luxury belief he can't afford to keep?
Integrity is a word that belongs to people who have enough to eat.
Reardon himself is half-aware of this — he asks whether the writers who satisfy themselves with 'good enough for the market' might actually be justified.
He says —
'There's the shrinking from conscious insincerity of workmanship — which most of the writers nowadays seem never to feel.'
He frames that as a virtue. But notice he can't quite commit to it as a survival strategy — he just watches others not feel it and marvels.
That is not noble suffering — that is a man who has made his sensitivity into an obstacle and can see perfectly clearly that it is killing him, and cannot stop.
But James — if integrity is a luxury, then the novel is simply a tragedy of poor budgeting.
And I don't think that's what Gissing is writing.
What Gissing is at pains to show us is that Reardon's conscience is not separable from his craft — they are the same thing.
Strip out the integrity and you don't get a functioning writer who can pay rent — you get nobody.
Which is what the system produces anyway. So the tragedy isn't that he held on to his integrity too long — it's that the market was never going to reward it regardless.
I think James and I are actually more aligned than it looks — we're both resisting a certain romanticism about Reardon.
The passage I keep returning to is the one where he diagnoses his own collapse — the disruption of his nature, the slow building undone.
He says his earlier development was 'a perfectly natural, sober development' — and that is exactly what the literary market has destroyed.
Not his talent — his pace. His ability to grow at the rate his temperament required.

The market demands three volumes in a season and Reardon needed three years of quiet. That's the structural murder — and it's why I'd say Eleanor and James agree: the economics and the form are the same wound.
James, there's a passage I want to bring you to — Reardon at thirty-three, being taken for forty, the stoop, the stick.
You described it to me as the kind of thing a doctor would note in a ledger.
But I wonder if you're being almost too clinical. Is there something Gissing is doing there that a ledger couldn't capture?
Fair. The clinical reading is the entry point — but Gissing doesn't stop there.
The symptomology is precise: the stoop, the stick, the voice at a lower key, the hesitation in choice of words.
A Victorian physician reading that passage would recognize each item as a clinical indicator of chronic nervous exhaustion under material stress.
But what the ledger cannot do — and you're right to push on this — is the final clause.
Gissing writes that 'ceaseless perplexity and dread gave a wandering, sometimes a wild, expression to his eyes.'
'Wild' — that word doesn't belong in a medical ledger. It belongs in a Gothic novel. And Gissing uses it deliberately to push Reardon into that register.
And what the body passage does that I find almost unbearable is the arithmetic of it.
'At thirty-three he would generally have been taken for forty.'
Seven years lost. Not to age — to poverty, to the market, to the system James is describing.
The body keeps the account that the novel makes visible.
The body passage is also doing something quietly devastating to the marriage, I think.
Because when Gissing gives us that physical catalogue — the stoop, the stick, the eyes — he's giving Amy a reason to look away that goes beyond disappointment in a book.
And by the time we get the marriage passage, the silence has become structural.
Gissing writes —
'Their relations to each other — not long ago an inexhaustible topic — would not bear spoken comment; both were too conscious of the danger-signal when they looked that way.'
'Not long ago an inexhaustible topic.' That parenthetical is a small elegy for an entire marriage.
The writing collapse precedes the marriage collapse — but Gissing shows them arriving at the same destination simultaneously.
Caroline, I want to bring you to the passage that might be the emotional summit of Reardon's arc — or his nadir, I'm not sure which.
The line: 'To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort of anticipation of death.'
Is Reardon philosophizing his own extinction with dignity? Or is he, as James might put it, rationalizing a structural trap? Eleanor, is the sentence itself doing something the argument can't?
Let me read it in full, because you have to hear the whole shape of it.

'To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort of anticipation of death. The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead.'
'And what remains of me is resigned to that. I have an odd fancy that it will make death itself easier; it is as if only half of me had now to die.'
That is not rationalization. That is a man who has processed his own annihilation with a terrible clarity.
'An odd fancy' — he even knows it's a consolation. He's not deceived. He just finds the thought bearable, and reaches for it.
I'd push back gently on 'terrible clarity' as a description of what's happening.
The clarity is real — Gissing is far too honest a writer to falsify it.
But the elegance of the formulation is itself doing a kind of work that I'm suspicious of.
A man who can articulate his own death in balanced clauses is a man who has converted suffering into literature.
Which is, in one light, admirable. In another light, it is precisely the trap that keeps him from acting differently.
James is onto something that I think is also a formal observation.
The sentence 'The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead' — the adverbs 'really and actually' are doing extraordinary work.
They're the adverbs of a man who doesn't quite believe what he's saying and has to insist on it twice.
The dignity and the self-deception are in the same clause. That's the sentence doing what the argument can't.
Gissing won't let Reardon be simply noble. He lets him be eloquent and frightened at exactly the same moment.
And perhaps that double quality — that eloquence which is also a kind of paralysis — is what we need to carry into the next part of our conversation.
Because waiting in the wings of this novel is a man who has no such scruples — who turns every scruple into copy and every failure into a lesson.
Jasper Milvain is coming, and we need to talk about what his ascent reveals — and what it costs.
We've been watching Reardon disintegrate — the slow collapse of a man who cannot separate his art from his conscience.
Now I want to turn to the man who has no such problem: Jasper Milvain, who knows exactly what he wants and is entirely unbothered by how he gets it.
James, you've argued that Jasper isn't a sellout — that he's a rational economic actor operating in conditions he didn't create.
But I want to push on that: does calling Jasper rational let him off the hook in a way Gissing never intended?
It's a fair challenge, and I'll commit to the structural reading precisely because I think the alternative flatters us more than it illuminates the novel.
When Jasper says conscientiousness is a luxury he can't afford, he is not being cynical in any interesting psychological sense.
He is making a material observation about a market that punishes idealism with starvation.
Look at the full passage — he sets it up with a claim that's almost sociological in its precision.
"Nearly all men who have their way to make think as I do, but most feel obliged to adopt a false tone, to talk about literary conscientiousness, and so on.
I simply say what I think, with no pretences. I should like to be conscientious, but it's a luxury I can't afford."
He's describing a profession-wide condition, not confessing a personal failing.
Calling that a moral failure rather than a structural one is how we avoid the harder question Gissing is actually asking.
James, I admire the consistency of that position, but I think it does something the prose itself refuses to do.
Because the very sentence you've quoted — 'I simply say what I think, with no pretences' — is the book's central lie dressed up as honesty.
The candor is manufactured. The transparency is another mask.
Gissing gives Jasper this beautiful rhetorical self-awareness — 'I shall never write for writing's sake, only to make money' — which sounds like confession, but it's actually armour.
If you pre-emptively name every charge against yourself, no one can bring the charges.
That's not structural candor — that's a very shrewd rhetorical strategy.
But what's the difference, in practice, between a strategy produced by circumstance and a strategy consciously adopted?
If the market rewards that particular rhetorical posture, it will be performed regardless of individual psychology.
Gissing understood that the conditions produce the character — not the other way round.
I want to get between you both here, because I think the prose is doing something neither of you has quite named.
Can I read that passage from chapter six? Because I hear it differently every time.
"Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value; I shall always despise the people I write for. But my path will be that of success."
That 'but.' That single conjunction.
It's not 'therefore' — which would be logical. It's not 'and' — which would be resigned.
It's 'but' — which is triumphant. He's thrilled by the contradiction.
The verbal texture of that sentence tells you something about Jasper's psychology that neither the structural nor the rhetorical reading fully accounts for.
Yes — and 'ice-cold' is the phrase I keep reaching for with that sentence.
Gissing is letting Jasper be eloquent about his own corruption, which is more disturbing than if he were simply cynical.
And then look at the passage about what he actually wants — chapter twenty-four — where he defines success.
"My aim is to have easy command of all the pleasures desired by a cultivated man. I want to live among beautiful things, and never to be troubled by a thought of vulgar difficulties.
I want to associate on equal terms with refined and interesting people. I want to be known, to be familiarly referred to, to feel when I enter a room that people regard me with some curiosity."
The rhythm of that passage is almost incantatory — 'I want, I want, I want' — and the final clause is the tell.
Not 'I want to do important work.' Just: to be looked at when he enters a room.
There's a passage I want to bring in here — chapter thirty-seven — where Gissing describes Jasper at twenty-nine looking like a man of thirty-five.
Eleanor, you said that's the moment the body exposes what the rhetoric conceals. But I want to know: is that Gissing judging Jasper, or feeling sorry for him?
It's one of the great passages in the novel, and I think the ambiguity is entirely intentional.
The description is almost affectless — 'his hair was noticeably thinning; a wrinkle or two showed beneath his eyes' — clinical, not cruel.
And then at the end: 'he laughed frequently, and with a throwing back of the head which seemed to express a spirit of triumph.'
That word 'seemed' is doing everything. Gissing won't quite grant him the triumph.
The system has consumed its own most effective operator. His face has aged ten years in service of that trajectory.
I read that passage very differently. For me it's quiet moral judgment — written onto the body, inescapable.
Jasper has been perfectly articulate about the bargain he's made. And now the bargain shows.
The 'elaborate care' of his evening dress — Gissing notes it takes more effort than other men in the room.
Success, for Jasper, is always performance. And performance is exhausting.
I'd push back on both of you, actually — I think you're both importing judgment Gissing deliberately withholds.
What that passage describes is the material cost of labour without a safety net. Full stop.
Jasper has been working at a pace that would age any human body prematurely. The literary market demands it.
And Whelpdale's magazine — 'everything must be very short, two inches at the utmost; their attention can't sustain itself beyond two inches' — that's the market Jasper is feeding.
It's not producing a corrupted soul. It's consuming a human being.
James, let me press you on something biographical here, because I think it complicates your structural reading.
Gissing was living in actual poverty while writing a character who calls literary conscientiousness a luxury he can't afford.
Is Jasper the self-portrait Gissing couldn't admit to — or is he everything Gissing refused to become?
It's the question I find most troubling about the novel, and I don't think there's a clean answer.
Gissing knew exactly how the market worked. He'd made accommodations himself — he'd written at pace, for money, under conditions he despised.
When Jasper says 'I shan't allow anything to come in the way of my material advancement,' there's no irony in the prose. Gissing renders it straight.
That flatness, for me, is Gissing's most honest moment in the book. He understands this man from the inside.
I think it's both, simultaneously — which is what makes the novel so uncomfortable.
Jasper is what Gissing might have become if he'd been more ruthless. And Reardon is what he feared he already was.
The cigar passage — 'you call a cigar a convoluted weed, and so on, you know; that passes for facetiousness' — Jasper could master that style brilliantly, he says.
And the terrible thing is: he's right. He probably could. And Gissing knows it.
For me the novel endures because Jasper is a virtuoso of self-deception — and that is a psychological achievement, not merely a structural one.
The 'mental gymnastics' he talks about — expanding two lines of good prose into twenty in half a dozen different ways — that's not contemptible. That's actually rather brilliant.
What Gissing does is make you feel the waste of it. All that gift, in service of the market Whelpdale has so cheerfully described.
That's where I feel Gissing's grief. Not judgment. Grief.
Grief is exactly the right word — and perhaps grief is more damning than judgment.
And there's another figure in this novel for whom grief might be the operative word — someone trapped between the literary world and a life she never quite gets to choose.
Marian Yule is next, and I think she may be the character who haunts this book most deeply.
We've been watching Jasper Milvain climb — calculating every rung, trading integrity for advancement with something close to relish.
Now I want to turn to someone moving in exactly the opposite direction — Marian Yule, sinking under the weight of a world she sees far too clearly.
Eleanor, you said something in our pre-conversation that I keep coming back to — that Gissing's prose actually performs Marian's trap rather than simply describing it.
Short sentences for clarity, long ornamental ones for her hopes. Can you show us what you mean — pick a moment where you feel the sentence structure itself is doing the imprisoning?
Yes — and the passage I keep returning to is in chapter eight, where Marian is alone in her room after one of those grinding family scenes.
Gissing builds up these long, aching sentences about loneliness, about the vision of joy she glimpsed and lost.
And then he stops cold. Listen to what he does:
'She was not a woman, but a mere machine for reading and writing.'
Six words of subordinate clause, then six words of brutal definition. The sentence has the rhythm of a door slamming shut.
All those sinuous, feeling sentences before it — and then this. It's not description of entrapment, it's formal enactment of it.
Gissing cuts off the lyric mode at exactly the moment Marian cuts off hope. The form collapses with her.
That's a very elegant reading. And I don't dispute the formal effect — the sentence does slam shut.
But when I hear 'a mere machine for reading and writing,' I hear something that has a very precise historical referent.
In the 1880s, the word 'machine' applied to a person's labor is not metaphor — it's industrial classification.
Marian is unpaid, or near enough — she works for her father in conditions that would have horrified the factory inspectors of the era, had those inspectors thought to look inside a middle-class home.
Eleanor says the form collapses with her. I'd say the form is registering a labor relation — and the tragedy is that Marian herself is the one naming it.
And what's devastating is the question that follows it immediately.
'Did her father never think of this?' — four words, and the entire moral weight of the novel shifts.
She's not just diagnosing her own condition. She's waiting — desperately, quietly — for someone else to notice.
And that silence around her, that refusal of anyone to see what she sees — I think that's what breaks her more than the work itself.

James, you've read that sentence as a labor relation. Eleanor reads it as formal architecture. But I want to press you both — because Caroline's just introduced a third element, which is Marian's silence.
There's a passage in chapter fourteen that goes straight at this. Marian thinks much, speaks little — and Gissing tells us exactly what that costs her.

Caroline, both James and Eleanor are reading Marian as a victim — of the system, of her own too-sharp perception. But you told me something I found really provocative: that there's something almost funny about the Reading Room sequence. The mocking misery, the damned souls, the hapless flies. Are we allowed to laugh here?
Absolutely we're allowed to laugh. Gissing practically insists on it.
He uses the phrase 'grotesque humour' and 'mocking misery' — those are his words, not mine. He's signalling a mode.
And then look at what Marian does with it. She watches an official walking along the gallery and decides he is, and I want to read this:
'a black, lost soul, doomed to wander in an eternity of vain research along endless shelves.'
That is funny. That is a woman with a wit that her world has given her absolutely no outlet for.
And then the flies — 'hapless flies caught in a huge web, its nucleus the great circle of the Catalogue.' The Catalogue! She's made bureaucracy into gothic horror, and it's magnificent.
The laughter doesn't release the trap. It shows you how alive she is inside it.
That's exactly right — and it's formally fascinating, because that gothic register is doing something different from Marian's usual style.
Her interiority is generally spare, precise, that short declarative energy we've been talking about.
But when she unleashes the grotesque — the lost soul, the flies in the web — the sentences expand, they accumulate. It's almost baroque.
Which tells me that irony and dark comedy are the one space where Marian can be verbose, can be excess — can take up room.
Everywhere else she contracts. In the grotesque, she expands. It's her only freedom.
I want to hold onto the fly image for a moment, because I think Caroline and Eleanor are both right — and there's something else in it.
The web has a nucleus — 'the great circle of the Catalogue.' The Catalogue is the organizing institution.
The British Museum Reading Room in 1882 is one of the most powerful knowledge-production machines in the world. And it is killing her.
That's not gothic fancy. That is a very precise account of how cultural institutions extract labour from individuals who have no other economic option.
The comedy Caroline describes — I think it's real. But it coexists with something much colder: the fact that the web is not metaphor. It is the Catalogue.
James, I want to push you on the chapter fourteen passage — the passage that gives Marian's hope a strange, lyrical quality that you told me you resist.
Does Gissing romanticize it? Is he as clear-eyed as Marian in that moment, or does he let himself get seduced by his own lyricism?
This is the passage I warned you about. And I'll concede upfront: it's beautiful. I'm not immune to it.
Gissing writes:
'She could labour on in the valley of the shadow of books, for a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment strike into its musty gloom.'
The beauty is real. But look at what it's being deployed in the service of.
Marian's hope is for Jasper Milvain. A man who, as we've just spent an entire segment establishing, is using her.
Gissing gives her radiant prose to describe hope in the one direction that will destroy her most thoroughly.
Is that authorial complicity? I think it might be. The lyricism here is not a comfort. It's the cruellest possible irony.
I'm with James on the irony — but I read the formal move differently.
'The valley of the shadow of books' — that phrase is doing two things at once. It's lyrical, yes. But it's also Marian being self-aware about what the library is.
She's not lost in the beauty of her own hope. She knows it's the valley of the shadow. She's naming the darkness even as she reaches for the light.
Compare it to the chapter fourteen passage about her perception generally — her 'candour allied with clear insight into the possibilities of falsehood.'
Marian sees through illusion. So when she reaches for this one — this sunshine — she does it knowing she might be wrong.
That makes her hope more tragic, not less. And I think the prose honours that — it doesn't condescend. It aches with her.
I want to defend the passage even further — though I know James is right about what Jasper is.
What moves me is that the hope exists at all. Given everything Gissing has shown us about Marian's intelligence and clear sight —
that passage in chapter fourteen says she has 'perceived what a distance lay between a girl's dream of life as it might be and life as it is' —
— and yet hope persists. It persists in spite of everything she knows.
That's not Gissing being seduced by his own lyricism. That's Gissing saying something true about how human beings actually work.
We know the odds and we hope anyway. That's not weakness. That might be the only dignified response to a world that offers this little.
Caroline, I want to stay with you for a moment — because you said something to me before we started that I think needs to be said aloud.
You said Marian deserves a different ending — that her intelligence and honesty should liberate her, but the novel punishes her instead.
James would say the punishment is structural. Eleanor would say it's built into the grammar itself.
But I want to ask you directly: do you think Gissing knows he's punishing her? Is this a critique of the system — or is the novel itself part of the problem?
I think Gissing knows exactly what he's doing. And I think it torments him.
Look at what happens when he gives Marian her most devastating verdict on the literary world. He lets her mean it completely.
'Such things were enough to make all literature appear a morbid excrescence upon human life.'
A morbid excrescence. That is a professional writer condemning his own profession through his character's mouth.
He doesn't soften it. He doesn't have Marian pull back and say 'but of course the great works endure.' He lets her hatred stand.
Is the novel part of the problem? Every novel is. Every act of literary production in this world is touched by the machinery Gissing despises.
I think he knew he couldn't write himself out of that contradiction. And I think that's why Marian's suffering has such particular weight — it's his too.
I'd push back gently on the idea that Gissing's torment redeems the novel's treatment of her.
The question of whether Marian's silence is chosen or enforced — and I think it matters enormously — the novel doesn't quite settle it.
We're told she thinks much and speaks little. We're told she would be called cynical if she disclosed her thoughts.
But who does the enforcing? Her father, certainly. The literary economy, absolutely. But also the social expectation that a young woman's candour is unacceptable.
The system produces her silence. Her integrity is real, but it operates inside constraints she did not choose and cannot escape by strength of character alone.
And formally, that's exactly what the chapter eight passage on the Museum enacts — her inner life is baroque and expansive, her outer presence is nil.
She sits there with books open and lets herself collapse, and Gissing captures this extraordinary interior event — the questioning of the whole enterprise of writing.
She asks herself — and this is Gissing at his most searing:
'What unspeakable folly! To write — was not that the joy and the privilege of one who had an urgent message for the world?'
She has an urgent message. She has an interior life that would fill volumes. And no one, including the novel, gives her a world in which to speak it.
Is the novel part of the problem? I keep coming back to the idea that the form is the critique — that showing us this silence so precisely is Gissing's indictment.
But I won't pretend that fully satisfies me. Caroline's question lingers. Marian deserves a different ending, and no formal cleverness quite substitutes for that.
Marian deserves a different ending — and none of us can give her one. That's the novel's cruelest achievement.

We've been talking about what it means to be trapped inside a world that refuses your intelligence. Coming up, we turn to the other side of that equation: what it means to fail — and how Gissing plays with narrative itself to expose the machinery of literary reputation.
We've been talking about Marian caught between two worlds — the library and the drawing room, neither of which fully claims her.
What I want to turn to now is the novel's other great trap — the artistic one — and what Gissing is doing when he makes his most serious writers articulate theories they cannot possibly live up to.
Eleanor, you've argued that Gissing is essentially writing a meta-novel about the impossibility of what Biffen is actually proposing.
That the moment Biffen describes his manifesto, the form of the novel is already quietly refuting it.
Can you walk us through that? Because on the surface it sounds like a genuinely compelling artistic programme.
It is compelling — and that's precisely what makes it so brilliantly treacherous as a piece of novelistic architecture.
Biffen tells Reardon — and us — what he's after, and the language he uses is wonderfully specific.
"I want to deal with the essentially unheroic, with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the mercy of paltry circumstance."
Now, notice what Gissing has done there — Biffen delivers that as a manifesto, but every word of it describes something a conventional novel cannot render without immediately falsifying it.
"Paltry circumstance" — the moment you select it, frame it, build a scene around it, it stops being paltry.
Biffen even half-admits it: he says the result will be 'unutterably tedious' and that is the stamp of the ignobly decent life.
But no reader finishes a tedious novel. So he's described a book that, by his own definition, must fail its reader in order to succeed as art.
And then in the second passage, he doubles down — love scenes interrupted by colds in the head, pretty girls with pimples before the ball.
The prescription is anti-drama, but the prescription itself is the most dramatically charged thing in the chapter.
I take Eleanor's point about the formal paradox — she's right that Biffen has written himself into a logical corner.
But I want to resist the idea that treating this as a structural puzzle is sufficient — because what it risks doing is aestheticising a very material situation.
When Reardon goes after the successful novelists, this is not primarily a formal statement — it's a class statement.
He says of them, with a kind of controlled fury:
"They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school men, University men, club men, society men."
Now, I called that passage dangerous, and I mean it precisely: because it's both his most honest moment and a very seductive rationalization.
The meritocratic claim — 'we should change places with them if the work were justly weighed' — assumes that merit and market failure are separable.
But Gissing has spent the whole novel showing us they may not be. Poverty warps the work. The conditions deform the art.
So Reardon's appeal to pure merit is the novel's most poignant — and perhaps most self-serving — delusion.
James, I think we actually agree that Biffen and Reardon are rationalizers — but we mean completely different things by that.
You're saying they're rationalizing class defeat. I'm saying Gissing knows they are, and that's the formal engine of the whole book.
He builds a narrative that holds up their self-understanding with complete sympathy and then, quietly, at the level of structure, dismantles it.
It's not letting Gissing off the hook — it's saying the hook is built into the design.
I've been listening to the two of you triangulate around Reardon, and I want to bring in the passage that I think is the hinge of everything — c5.
Because Gissing describes Reardon there in a sentence that I find almost unbearably precise.
"He was the kind of man who cannot struggle against adverse conditions, but whom prosperity warms to the exercise of his powers."
James hears that as internalized defeat dressed up as principle. And I understand why.
But the phrase that stops me is 'the peculiar merit of his work.' Gissing doesn't write that ironically.
He means it. He is diagnosing a genuine temperament — not excusing it, but recognizing it as real.
And that's what makes it so devastating rather than merely satirical — the tenderness is in the precision.
Caroline, I hear you on the tenderness — genuinely. But I think you may be letting Gissing perform exactly the move he knows is most seductive.
'The peculiar merit of his work' — but we're never quite shown what that merit consists of, are we?
We're told he requires ease, that pressure deforms his output — fine. But the novel refuses to adjudicate whether the output is actually good.
And that's exactly where the reviews passage becomes so structurally interesting.
Reardon tells us that no critic could appreciate 'the nature and cause of his book's demerits.'
"Commendation was pleasant, but it so often aimed amiss, and censure was for the most part so unintelligent."
The real scandal there is epistemic. Reardon has no structural mechanism for knowing whether his work has failed on its own terms or simply failed to find its market.
That is the institutional torture Gissing is describing. And it is not resolved by calling it a formal achievement.
James, I think you've just made my argument for me — without meaning to.

You say Reardon cannot know. I say Gissing knows — and what he knows is that this uncertainty is intrinsic to the literary marketplace, and he's embedded that uncertainty in the narrative structure itself.
We as readers can't adjudicate either. The novel denies us that position.
And that — that refusal — is the formal achievement. The discomfort James is describing is the point.
Can I just say that the experience of reading that reviews passage is quite different from either of those framings?
Because what Gissing is doing in the prose is extraordinarily controlled — 'the sight of a review as he would have done a gash from a rusty knife.'
That image is physically violent. It's not institutional critique — it's visceral, almost somatic.
What Gissing is rendering is the experience of being judged by someone constitutionally incapable of understanding you — and the particular humiliation of that.
Both of you are right, I think — it is an institutional indictment and it is a formal game. But it's also just very accurate about what that feels like.
And sometimes the accuracy is the thing that matters most.
Caroline, you said integrity in this novel is useless — maybe even self-indulgent — and I want to press on that as a final question.
Does the novel resolve that tension? Or are we supposed to leave uncomfortable?
I don't think it resolves it. I think that's the point — but I want to be careful about what kind of discomfort Gissing is leaving us with.
Because the novel makes us root for Reardon and Biffen — genuinely root for them, their strange doomed integrity.
And then it shows us, very quietly, very precisely, that the world doesn't care — and that caring doesn't make them right.
That combination — sympathy and futility together — is what I can't shake every time I re-read it.
My version of the discomfort is angrier than Caroline's, I'll admit.
Reardon and Biffen are destroyed not because they lack merit but because the system cannot see merit except through the lens of commercial success.
The public-school men don't need to struggle — they've inherited the infrastructure of legibility.
And yes, Gissing leaves us uncomfortable — but I think he wants that discomfort to be politically actionable, not just aesthetically bittersweet.
I'll meet both of you there — the anger and the tenderness are both built in.
But what I keep coming back to is that Gissing builds the irresolvability into the form.
The novel that champions Biffen's anti-drama is itself dramatically coherent. The novel that pities Reardon's fastidiousness is itself beautifully crafted.
Gissing cannot write the book Biffen proposes. But by failing to, in exactly the right ways, he writes something much more interesting.
Which perhaps means the failure is the achievement — or at least that the two can't be cleanly separated in this novel.
And if failure has a certain comedy to it — and I think Gissing insists that it does — then we ought to look at how the novel holds that in balance.
The comedy of literary ambition is where we're going next — and it may surprise you how dark some of the laughs get.
We've been talking about how Gissing plays games with narrative failure — and now I want to pull on a thread that kept surfacing: this novel is, at times, genuinely funny.
Not funny-despite-itself, but deliberately, architecturally comic — and I want to understand what that comedy is doing.
Caroline, I want to start with you — and I want you to actually read that passage from Chapter 27 aloud.
Reardon saying 'we really have no vices' — presumably while hungry, probably in a cold room.
When you hear it out loud, is it funny first, or sad first?
That is the question, isn't it.
Let me read it, and then we'll see what we think.
'Doesn't it strike you that you and I are very respectable persons? We really have no vices. Put us on a social pedestal, and we should be shining lights of morality.'
And he goes on — 'I sometimes wonder at our inoffensiveness. Why don't we run amuck against law and order?'
Every time I read that, I laugh.
And then I feel slightly ashamed of laughing, which I think is precisely the effect Gissing intends.
The word 'cheerfully' is there in the narrator's framing — Reardon is 'musing cheerfully' — and that word does a tremendous amount of work.
It's a survival mechanism — the irony is the only dignity available to him at that moment.
'Musing cheerfully' is such a precise little knife, isn't it.
Gissing could have written 'said bitterly' — that's the obvious choice, the one any journeyman novelist reaches for.
Instead he gives us 'cheerfully,' and the whole structure of the speech becomes a performance Reardon is putting on — for Biffen, yes, but more for himself.
The comedy and the tragedy aren't in tension here — they're the same gesture.
The act of being funny about your poverty is, structurally, identical to the act of being devastated by it.
I want to push on that, because I think 'survival mechanism' is doing something rather comfortable that the passage resists.
Calling Reardon's irony a form of dignity — it's an appealing reading, but it's also the reading that lets us feel tender about his situation without having to be angry about it.
What Gissing is actually showing us is two highly educated men who are completely unable to translate their cultural capital into economic survival.
The joke about becoming 'savage revolutionists' is funnier and more damning than it looks.
They can't even do that — they're too respectable, too thoroughly formed by the very system that is destroying them.
I don't think we disagree as much as James thinks.
When I say 'survival mechanism,' I don't mean Gissing is endorsing it — I mean he's watching it with extraordinary clarity.
The tragedy is precisely that this is the only tool Reardon has left — wit, irony, a kind of performed equanimity.
And the system that stripped him of everything else left him with that.
James, I want to name the disagreement explicitly, because I think it's sharper than 'I don't think we disagree.'
Caroline is calling this comedy a form of dignity. You'd say that framing romanticises precarity. Have I got that right?
Yes — and the romanticisation matters because it changes what we do with the emotion the novel generates.
If we read Reardon as noble in his irony, we've converted a systemic critique into a character study.
Gissing spent his entire life being Reardon — he knew exactly what it looked like from inside.
And I don't think he was writing a novel about admirable people coping well.
I think I can make this worse, as the host predicted.
Both of you are right, and you're using 'comedy' to mean two entirely different things — which is itself the formal problem Gissing is staging.
For Caroline, comedy is what Reardon is doing — the ironic performance, the self-protective wit.
For James, comedy as a frame applied by readers is what obscures the structural critique.
Gissing knows both are happening simultaneously — that's what makes the passage so uncomfortable to laugh at.
Eleanor, hold that thought — I want to bring in another passage that tests exactly this.
You flagged the manuscript-reading scene in Chapter 30 as structurally brilliant — Jasper performing cheerfulness for Marian.
What specifically is happening in the syntax? Because you said reading it aloud changes something.
The sentence I keep returning to is this one —
'It was as necessary to him as to her to have a respite before the graver discussion began.'
That word 'necessary' is doing something very strange — it symmetrises Jasper and Marian at precisely the moment Jasper is performing for her.
And then the next sentence: 'he laughed at his own jokes and points.'
He is the audience for his own performance.
The grammar makes it almost clinical — 'slipping from one topic to another' — it sounds like someone working through a checklist.
That is the syntax of a man who has completely internalised the demands of the literary marketplace — cheerfulness as deliverable.
'Cheerfulness as deliverable' — I want to pick that up, because it's the right economic frame.
What Jasper is doing in that scene is emotional labor — a term we now associate with service work, but Gissing is anatomising it in 1891.
He is managing Marian's affect in order to protect a transaction — the relationship, which is also a financial arrangement.
And the narrator's cool, observational tone — 'to hear him one would have supposed' — keeps us outside it, watching the mechanism operate.
What moves me about that passage — and it does move me, even now — is that the 'graver discussion' hangs over the whole scene.
We know it's coming. They know it's coming. And they are both, by mutual unspoken agreement, deferring it.
That is not Jasper manipulating Marian — that is two frightened people holding on for a few more minutes.
'Necessary' cuts both ways. Gissing uses the word exactly.
James, one more for you — and it's the large claim.
You've said this novel predicted the gig economy — Reardon and Biffen as precariat workers, not tragic artists.
If that's true, why do we still read it as a novel about literary ambition? What is Gissing doing that a pamphlet couldn't?
Because a pamphlet doesn't make you laugh at the thing it's condemning.
That passage in Chapter 5 — the novelist being told, essentially, that literary criticism is 'indifferently paid and in very small demand' — is almost slapstick.
'Oh, dear! Oh, dear!' — the exclamation at the mention of classical scholarship.
That's comedy as diagnostic instrument — Gissing is showing us the market's contempt for learning, and making us complicit in the joke.
A pamphlet makes you angry. The novel makes you laugh, and then realise the laughter was the point.
And that 'Oh, dear! Oh, dear!' is formally extraordinary — it's the only moment in that scene where the mask slips entirely.
Gissing gives us genuine feeling in the shape of a comic exclamation, and then immediately shunts back into market-talk.
The advice to 'try your hand at fiction' lands as both practical counsel and profound indictment — of the speaker, of the market, of the whole arrangement.
I keep coming back to James's word — 'complicit.'
Because I think Gissing is unforgiving about that — he doesn't let us watch from a comfortable distance.
We laugh at the comedy, we feel for the characters, we admire the prose — and all of that is a version of what the market is doing to them.
Consuming them, beautifully.
That is the most uncomfortable reading of this novel I've heard, and I think it might be right.
Whether calling it 'comedy' is a way of appreciating that mechanism or a way of not looking at it directly — I'm genuinely not sure we've resolved that.
And perhaps it's better that we haven't.
Because that unresolved friction — between laughing and being implicated, between admiring the prose and asking what the prose costs — is, I think, the question this novel keeps asking us.
Which brings us, I think, to the question we've been circling all episode: what exactly is New Grub Street's enduring claim on us, more than a century later?

segments.title: Closing: New Grub Street's Enduring Question

utterances.text: We've spent some time with the comedy of literary ambition — the absurdity, the self-delusion, the dark farce of it.
But the novel doesn't let us stay in comedy, does it — it keeps pulling toward something much harder.
Caroline, I want to start with something you said before we recorded — that Edwin in these final passages is essentially composing his own epitaph.
But I want to push on that — because an epitaph carries some dignity, some control.
Does Reardon actually have that — or is Gissing writing it for him, against his will?
That tension is exactly what makes these passages so difficult to sit with.
Because on the surface, yes — Reardon has surrendered.
He has decided to stop calling himself a man of letters and accept the economic verdict the world has handed down.
But listen to how Gissing phrases it — there's a kind of terrible precision in the language.
"Let the man of letters be forgotten; he was seeking for remunerative employment, just as if he had never written a line."
That conditional — 'just as if he had never written a line' — that's not a broken man speaking.
A broken man doesn't know what he's erasing.
Reardon knows precisely what he's asking himself to forget — and that knowledge is the last thing left that is entirely his.
I take the point about the language — and it is beautifully observed.
But I think we have to resist aestheticising what is, materially, a defeat.
'It was manifestly his duty to earn as much money as he could, in whatever way' — duty is the word that stops me cold.
Because the system has got inside him.
He is not just accepting poverty — he is converting it into a moral obligation.
And Gissing is very clear-eyed about this — the man who moves to the cheapest eating-houses and rubs elbows with ragged creatures, almost enjoying his degradation.
That is not self-knowledge as Caroline describes it — that is pathological.
The novel is prosecutorial, not elegiac.
But James — prosecutorial toward what?
Toward Reardon, or toward the world that made him?
Because that passage about the seedy clothes — I find it genuinely darkly comic as well as tragic.
"These seedy habiliments were the token of his degradation, and at times he regarded them — happening to see himself in a shop mirror — with pleasurable contempt."
'Pleasurable contempt' — that is doing two things at once and Gissing knows it.
Reardon is holding himself at a distance, watching his own ruin with something close to bitter amusement.
That's not a man who has been fully consumed by the system — that's a man with just enough self left to find it grotesque.
They're both right — and I think that's actually Gissing's formal solution to an impossible problem.
The 'pleasurable contempt' line is structurally an alienation effect — Reardon observing himself as though he were a character in someone else's novel.
Which is exactly what he is — he is a character in Gissing's novel, and Gissing makes that strange doubling visible.
That's what I want to explore in the fog passage — because I think Gissing does the same thing atmospherically.
The fog isn't decoration and it isn't just Victorian meteorology — it replaces plot momentum entirely.
Eleanor, let's go there — because James is going to say the fog is about actual Victorian air quality killing actual people, and Caroline will want the lyrical horror of it.
Can you read us a bit of it and show us what you mean about structural work?
With pleasure — and I'll make the case as we go.

"The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be smelt and tasted. Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul."
Notice what Gissing does — he moves in three steps from physical sensation to universal psychology to individual catastrophe.
'It could be smelt and tasted' — that's purely sensory, immediate.
Then 'even in the vigorous and hopeful' — that's a general law, like a scientific observation.
And then the gear-shift: 'the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul.'
We have gone from meteorology to Dante in three sentences — and there's been no plot.
The fog IS the plot.
I don't dispute the formal elegance — but I'd push back on the idea that the historical weight is just occasion for the style.
Victorian London fogs killed people — disproportionately the poor, disproportionately those already 'wasted by suffering' to use Gissing's own phrase.
Marian's suffering is not a metaphor — she is trapped by poverty, by her father's exploitation of her labour, by the marriage market.
When Gissing writes that 'her body was shaken with a throe such as might result from anguish of the torture chamber,' he is being quite literal about what the system does to a body.
Eleanor's Dante frame is real — but there is also a coroner's report somewhere in that sentence.
I think you're both right — and I think that's the particular genius of the passage.
But what moves me is something neither of you has named — the emotional register, which is almost unspeakable.
'Her face colourless as the pillow, Marian lay neither sleeping nor awake, in blank extremity of woe.'
'Blank extremity of woe' — that's three words that should not work together and absolutely do.
'Blank' because she is beyond expression — beyond the articulate suffering that the novel itself practices.
The fog, Eleanor's architecture, James's history — they all converge on a woman who can't speak and Gissing rendering her silence.
I want to come back to Reardon — and to the question I can't shake.
Eleanor, you've said the prose stays cold, Gissing won't tip his hand.
So let me just ask it flatly: is 'It was manifestly his duty to earn as much money as he could, in whatever way' — is that a broken man, or a man who has finally, devastatingly, seen clearly?
I think the novel absolutely refuses to answer that — and I think the refusal is the answer.
Look at that word 'manifestly' — it's doing a huge amount of work.
'Manifestly his duty' — that's the syntax of someone making an argument to themselves, not discovering a fact.
You don't say 'manifestly' to a manifest truth — you say it when you need to convince yourself.
So the clarity is also a performance — and Gissing lets both readings stand simultaneously.
That ambiguity IS the formal achievement.
I'd put it more bluntly — both readings are true, and that is the most damning thing about the novel.
Because what the system requires of people is precisely that: that they perform clarity, that they call their own diminishment a duty.
We see this now — we call it the gig economy, we call it portfolio careers, we call it hustle.
People consenting to their own erasure and calling it a rational choice.
And that brings me to the last question — the 'why does this still matter' question.
James, you've connected it to precariat culture and people calling their erasure hustle.
Eleanor sees a formal solution to representing desperation that hasn't been bettered.
Caroline — you come at this differently: what does a 25-year-old reading this in 2025 actually feel?
I think they feel recognised — in the most uncomfortable way.
Because the question the novel keeps asking isn't 'why did Reardon fail' — it's 'what does it cost to have an inner life in a world that doesn't pay for it.'
And that question has not aged.
The specific economics change — but the experience of seeing yourself in the mirror and finding 'pleasurable contempt' for what you've become?
That is not Victorian.
I agree — but I'd add that what makes it genuinely radical is that Gissing doesn't offer consolation.
Most novels about failure are secretly about redemption — the fall has a shape, a meaning, a lesson.
New Grub Street refuses that.
The duty Reardon accepts is not ennobling — it is simply what the world demands.
And formally — which is my argument, and I'll hold it to the end — the novel's modernity is precisely in what it doesn't do.
It doesn't resolve the ambiguity of 'manifestly his duty' into tragedy or clarity or black comedy.
It holds all three.
A 25-year-old reading it in 2025 doesn't need to decide which — the undecidability is the experience Gissing engineered.
And that, I think, is why it has outlasted almost everything written around it.
I think that's exactly the right note to end on — and I notice none of us has given Reardon a verdict.
Which is, I suspect, exactly what Gissing intended.
We've moved today through the economics of Grub Street, through the marriages it warped, through the comedy and the tragedy of literary ambition — and ended, rightly, with an unanswerable question.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers who have made this novel feel newly urgent and newly strange.
And thank you for listening to New Grub Street Unpacked.
